title-group.article-title: Development and internal validation of a six-gene prognostic model based on galactose metabolism for overall survival in lung adenocarcinoma

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Lung cancer remains a leading cause of cancer incidence and mortality globally. Metabolic reprogramming promotes tumor progression and shapes an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Galactose metabolism is involved in multiple malignancies, but its prognostic value in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) remains unclear. This study aimed to develop and internally validate a galactose metabolism-related multigene prognostic model for LUAD.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A retrospective prognostic model development and internal validation study was performed using RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) and clinical data from 585 LUAD patients in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). Differential expression, functional enrichment, univariate and multivariate Cox regression were applied to construct a prognostic gene signature. Internal validation was performed using bootstrap resampling. Model performance was evaluated by time-dependent receiver operating characteristic (ROC), C-index, calibration, and Kaplan-Meier analysis. Associations between the model and immune infiltration, immunotherapy responsiveness, and tumor stemness were also analyzed.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A six-gene prognostic model (GALT, GANC, PGM1, GALM, B4GALT1, PGM2) was developed. The model showed good discrimination with 1-, 3-, and 5-year area under the curve (AUC) values of 0.719, 0.693, and 0.684, respectively. The low-risk group exhibited significantly longer survival, increased antitumor immune infiltration (CD8+ T cells, M1 macrophages, activated CD4+ memory T cells), higher expression of T cell proliferation-related genes, lower immune checkpoint expression, better predicted immunotherapy response, and lower tumor stemness compared with the high-risk group.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: We developed and internally validated a six-gene prognostic model for LUAD based on galactose metabolism. The model shows moderate prognostic performance and is associated with antitumor immunity and tumor stemness. It may be used for prognostic risk stratification and to guide personalized immunotherapy in LUAD.
Keywords: Galactose metabolism, lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), tumor immunity, prognostic model
Received 2026 Mar 25; Accepted 2026 Jul 1; Issue date 2026 Aug 31.

sec.title: Key findings
sec.p: • We established a prognostic model for lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) using 6 galactose metabolism-related genes (GALT, GANC, PGM1, GALM, B4GALT1, PGM2). Low-risk patients showed stronger anti-tumor immune infiltration, higher T-cell proliferation gene expression, lower immune checkpoint expression, better immunotherapy response, and lower tumor stemness.

sec.title: What is known and what is new?
sec.p: • Galactose metabolism is linked to cancers; metabolic reprogramming shapes tumor immunity and stemness.
• This is the first galactose metabolism-based prognostic signature for LUAD that links galactose gene patterns to immune infiltration, immunotherapy sensitivity, and tumor stemness.

sec.title: What is the implication, and what should change now?
sec.p: • This signature enables personalized prognosis and immunotherapy guidance for LUAD. Future studies should validate these genes experimentally and test them in clinical immunotherapy practice.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Globally, lung cancer caused nearly 2.5 million new cases and over 1.8 million deaths in 2022, making it a leading cause of cancer-related mortality and incidence (1). However, a substantial proportion of patients receive a diagnosis of lung cancer at an advanced stage, precluding the opportunity for curative surgical intervention and necessitating reliance on radiotherapy, chemotherapy, or targeted therapies aimed at inhibiting tumor progression. Despite advances in surgery, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, the prognosis of lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) patients remains highly heterogeneous. Reliable prognostic tools are urgently needed to stratify patient risk, predict survival, and guide personalized treatment strategies (2).

Compared to normal cells, the abnormal proliferation, survival, and cell fate control of tumor cells are regulated by cellular metabolism or specific metabolites (3). Metabolic reprogramming is a core hallmark of cancer. Prior investigations have elucidated that both neoplastic cells and stromal constituents within tumor microenvironments manifest metabolic traits akin to those of actively proliferating cells. Specifically, tumor cells demonstrate a propensity towards aerobic glycolysis, wherein glucose undergoes enzymatic conversion to lactic acid despite the presence of oxygen, instead of being fully oxidized to carbon dioxide. This phenomenon, recognized as aerobic glycolysis or the Warburg effect, underscores the metabolic reprogramming characteristic of tumorigenesis (4). In addition to the glycolytic phenotype, cancer cells exhibit significant alterations in lipid metabolism, encompassing fatty acid synthesis, β-oxidation, and cellular lipid composition (5). Furthermore, amino acid metabolism is frequently disrupted in cancer cells during tumorigenesis and progression (6). These intrinsic metabolic dysregulations collectively foster a tumor microenvironment characterized by high acidity, nutrient deprivation, and hypoxia. Such conditions further intensify the metabolic reprogramming observed in both tumor cells and immune cells within the tumor microenvironment (7). Changes in tumor metabolism are a major cause of impaired function in tumor-infiltrating immune cells. Metabolic reprogramming of glucose and lipid metabolism in tumors regulates the infiltration and functional states of immune cells through nutritional competition, signal transduction, and other mechanisms, severely affecting tumor progression (8,9).

In addition to glycolysis and lipid metabolism, galactose metabolism regulates tumor proliferation, immune infiltration, and cancer stemness. As an essential carbohydrate in cellular metabolism, galactose is one of the most abundant sugars in the human diet (10). It plays an essential role in energy production and storage across various human tissues and is involved in glycosylation. Galactosylated glycoconjugates, such as glycoproteins, keratan sulfate-containing proteoglycans, and glycolipids, serve multiple biological functions, including structural support, cell adhesion, and intracellular signaling (11). However, few studies have focused on the prognostic value of galactose metabolism-related genes in LUAD, and no robust prognostic model has been established based on this pathway.

This study aimed to develop and internally validate a multigene prognostic model based on galactose metabolism-related genes for LUAD. Using The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) cohort, we constructed a six-gene signature and evaluated its performance in predicting overall survival (OS). We further analyzed its associations with immune infiltration, immunotherapy responsiveness, and tumor stemness. This model may serve as a novel biomarker for prognostic stratification and immunotherapy guidance in LUAD. We present this article in accordance with the TRIPOD reporting checklist (available at https://tcr.amegroups.com/article/view/10.21037/tcr-2026-0696/rc).

sec.title: Study design, data source, participants and outcome
sec.p: The overall study workflow is shown in Figure 1. This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and its subsequent amendments. This was a retrospective prognostic model development and internal validation study. Gene expression RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data with survival follow-up information of 585 LUAD samples (including a small number of adjacent normal tissue samples) and normal tissue from TCGA database were downloaded (https://www.cancer.gov/ccg/research/genome-sequencing/tcga) (12). Raw data were normalized by log2(FPKM + 1) transformation. The inclusion criteria and exclusion criteria are as follows. Inclusion criteria were: (I) histologically confirmed LUAD; (II) available RNA-seq expression data; (III) complete OS time and survival status. Exclusion criteria were: (I) non-adenocarcinoma histological type; (II) missing survival time or key clinical variables (age, sex, or TNM stage). After applying these criteria, 490 LUAD patients were retained for prognostic model construction and survival analysis.

caption.p: Flowchart of the study. DEGGs, differentially expressed galactose metabolism-related genes; DEGs, differentially expressed genes; FC, fold change; GSEA, gene set enrichment analysis; LUAD, lung adenocarcinoma; ROC, receiver operating characteristic; ssGSEA, single-sample gene set enrichment analysis; TIDE, Tumor Immune Dysfunction and Exclusion.

sec.p: For external validation, an independent microarray dataset GSE31210, comprising 226 LUAD patients with complete gene expression profiles and clinical survival information, was retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/) database. Corresponding clinical information, including age, sex, and pathological stage (TNM stage) was extracted from the GEO database and the original study. To ensure comparability, the expression values of the six prognostic genes in GSE31210 were log2-transformed and z-score standardized prior to risk score calculation.

The primary outcome was OS, defined as the time from initial diagnosis to death from any cause. Patients who were alive at the last follow-up were defined as censored. All eligible patients with complete data were included, and the events-per-variable (EPV) ratio was greater than 10, meeting the statistical requirement for prognostic modeling. No missing data were observed for key variables, and complete-case analysis was performed.

All pathways related to galactose metabolism were collected from the Molecular Signatures Database (https://www.gsea-msigdb.org), and the genes within these pathways were compiled into a gene set consisting of 32 genes, named the galactose metabolism-related gene set (Table S1).

sec.title: Differential expression analysis
sec.p: Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between LUAD and normal tissues were identified using the “edgeR” R package (13). Thresholds were set as |log2FC| >1 and adjusted P<0.05. The intersection between DEGs and galactose metabolism-related genes was recognized as differentially expressed galactose metabolism-related genes (DEGGs) and visualized using a Venn diagram (14).

sec.title: Functional enrichment analysis and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA)
sec.p: Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses were performed using the “clusterProfiler” R package (15). Adjusted P<0.05 was considered statistically significant.

GSEA was performed using the “GSEABase” R package. Genes were ranked by log2FC in descending order. Pathways with |normalized enrichment score (NES)| >1 and P<0.05 were considered significantly enriched.

sec.title: Prognostic model construction
sec.p: The Cox regression model is an effective statistical method for analyzing censored survival data (12). DEGGs were evaluated using a univariate Cox regression model to investigate the impact on patients’ OS. In the results, genes with P<0.2 were identified as potential predictive markers. These genes, along with their P value, hazard ratios (HRs), and 95% confidence intervals (CIs), were represented in the corresponding forest plot. Then, multivariate Cox proportional hazard regression was conducted to construct a predictive risk model utilizing the “survival” R package (16). The risk score for each patient was calculated as a linear combination of the expression levels of the six prognostic genes weighted by their respective multivariate Cox regression coefficients (βᵢ), as follows:

where Xᵢ represents the normalized expression value [log2(FPKM + 1)] of the i-th gene, and βᵢ represents the corresponding regression coefficient derived from the multivariate Cox model. A positive coefficient indicates a risk factor (higher expression associated with poorer prognosis), whereas a negative coefficient indicates a protective factor (higher expression associated with better prognosis).

By incorporating various predictive and influencing factors to create personalized likelihoods of medical outcomes, nomograms satisfy our need for biologically and clinically integrated models and support the advancement of personalized medicine (13). To further visualize the predictive model we developed, a nomogram was constructed utilizing genes identified via multivariate Cox regression analysis to estimate the 1-, 3-, and 5-year OS probabilities in patients with LUAD by the “rms” R package (17).

In addition to using these genes to construct a model for comprehensively evaluating their importance in predicting patient survival, we also assessed the individual association of these prognostic genes with patient survival using Kaplan-Meier curves and log-rank tests.

sec.title: Validation, risk stratification and model performance
sec.p: Internal validation was performed using bootstrap resampling (1,000 iterations) to evaluate model stability and reduce overfitting. Model performance was evaluated using the concordance index (C-index), time-dependent receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves at 1, 3, and 5 years, calibration curves, and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis with log-rank test (18). Patients were divided into high-risk and low-risk groups using the median risk score as the cutoff. Distribution of risk scores, survival status, and gene expression patterns were visualized using scatter plots and heatmaps.

To further validate the generalizability of the prognostic model, the six-gene risk score formula derived from the TCGA training cohort was applied to the independent GSE31210 validation cohort. Risk scores for GSE31210 patients were calculated using the identical regression coefficients (β) and standardized gene expression values. Patients in the GSE31210 cohort were stratified into high-risk and low-risk groups based on the median risk score of the GSE31210 cohort. Time-dependent ROC analysis [1-, 3-, and 5-year area under the curve (AUC)] and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis with log-rank tests were performed to evaluate the predictive performance of the model in the external validation cohort. Meanwhile, the response to immunotherapy was validated in the GSE126044 dataset.

sec.title: Immune infiltration, immune checkpoint and immunotherapy analysis
sec.p: CIBERSORT algorithm (19) determines the cellular makeup of complex tissues by gene expression data. This algorithm was used to analyze the infiltration proportions of 22 immune cells in the tumor tissues of each LUAD patient. Following this, we used the Wilcoxon rank-sum test to compare the proportions of immune cells infiltrating the two groups.

Expression levels of 41 immune checkpoint genes, 16 T-cell proliferation driver genes and 5 T-cell exhaustion markers genes were compared between groups (Table S1). Immunotherapy responsiveness was evaluated using the Tumor Immune Dysfunction and Exclusion (TIDE) algorithm (20).

sec.title: Tumor stemness analysis
sec.p: Tumor stemness indices were calculated according to previously published methods (21). Expression levels of stemness-related genes were compared between high-risk and low-risk groups (Table S1). All comparisons were performed using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test.

sec.title: Immunohistochemistry image acquisition from public databases
sec.p: Representative immunohistochemistry images of aimed proteins in normal lung tissue and LUAD tumor tissue were retrieved from the Human Protein Atlas (HPA, version 23.0, accessed January 2025). All HPA images are publicly reusable with direct source links listed in Figure S1, in accordance with HPA data reuse guidelines (22).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.3.1). Kaplan-Meier curves with log-rank test were used for survival comparison. Univariate and multivariate Cox regression were used to identify prognostic factors. A two-sided P<0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Immune responses and extracellular structures differentiate LUAD from normal tissues
sec.p: A total of 9,224 DEGs were identified between LUAD and normal tissues at the mRNA level (Figure 2A). GO and KEGG enrichment analyses demonstrated that DEGs were mainly enriched in biological processes including humoral immune response, cell/phagocytosis recognition, and extracellular structure; cellular components including immunoglobulin complex and ion channel complex; and molecular functions including channel activity, receptor/ligand activity and antigen binding (Figure 2B). By intersecting DEGs with 32 galactose metabolism-related genes, we obtained 12 DEGGs (Figure 2C).

caption.p: Galactose metabolism, immune responses, and extracellular structures differentiate LUAD from normal tissues. (A) Volcano plot of LUAD. (B) KEGG enrichment and GO enrichment results of DEGs. (C) DEGGs are genes shared by DEGs and galactose genes. DEGGs, differentially expressed galactose metabolism-related genes; DEGs, differentially expressed genes; FC, fold change; GO, Gene Ontology; KEGG, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes; LUAD, lung adenocarcinoma; TCGA, The Cancer Genome Atlas.

sec.title: DEGGs profoundly influence the survival of LUAD patients
sec.p: According to the varying expression levels of genes related to galactose metabolism in LUAD versus normal tissues, we propose two key questions: 1) Is there an association between galactose metabolism-related genes and patient survival? 2) Can the expression of these genes predict the survival outcomes of LUAD patients? To explore these questions, TCGA-LUAD data on survival time and status, along with gene expression profiles, were examined. Univariate Cox regression analysis was performed to evaluate the prognostic value of 12 DEGGs. Nine genes with P<0.2 were selected for subsequent multivariate Cox regression (Figure 3A). A six-gene prognostic model was established, including GALT, GANC, PGM1, GALM, B4GALT1, and PGM2 (Figure 3B). Among these, GALT, GANC, PGM1, and GALM were protective factors (HR <1), while B4GALT1 and PGM2 were risk factors (HR >1). Kaplan-Meier survival analysis confirmed that high expression of B4GALT1 and PGM2 was associated with shorter OS, while high expression of GANC and PGM1 was associated with longer OS (Figure 3C). A nomogram was constructed to predict 1, 3, and 5-year OS probabilities (Figure 3D).

caption.p: DEGGs profoundly influence the survival of LUAD patients. (A) The forest plot of 9 DEGGs in LUAD (P<0.2) by univariate Cox. (B) The forest plot of 6 DEGGs in LUAD filtered by multivariate Cox. (C) Kaplan-Meier curves of the 6 DEGGs in LUAD. (D) Development of a nomogram to predict 1-, 3-, and 5-year overall survival probabilities for LUAD patients. CI, confidence interval; DEGGs, differentially expressed galactose metabolism-related genes; HR, hazard ratio; LUAD, lung adenocarcinoma; OS, overall survival.

sec.title: Prognostic model based on DEGGs shows predictive performance
sec.p: To determine the risk score for each LUAD patient, we used a prognostic model where a higher risk score correlates with a greater risk of death and a poorer prognosis, whereas a lower risk score suggests a better prognosis. All 585 LUAD patients were stratified into low-risk and high-risk groups using the median risk score as the cutoff. In the riskscore-Low group, four protective factors were highly expressed, while in the riskscore-High group, two risk factors were highly expressed (Figure 4A). The time-dependent ROC analysis confirmed the model’s predictive reliability, with AUC values of 0.719, 0.693, and 0.684 for OS at 1, 3, and 5 years, respectively (Figure 4B). The high-risk group had significantly shorter OS than the low-risk group (P=1.5×106) (Figure 4C). Multivariate Cox regression analysis further demonstrated that the risk score remained an independent prognostic factor after adjusting for age, sex, and pathological stage (Figure 4D).

caption.p: Prognostic model by DEGGs shows good predictive performance for LUAD patients. (A) Risk factor correlation chart of 6 DEGGs in riskscore-high and riskscore-low groups. (B) Time ROC in LUAD patients. (C) Kaplan-Meier curves in LUAD patients with riskscore-high and riskscore-low groups. (D) Multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression forest plot showing the independent prognostic value of the risk score after adjusting for age, sex, and pathological stage. (E) Time-dependent ROC curves for overall survival at 1, 3, and 5 years in the external GSE31210 validation cohort (AUC =0.709, 0.691, and 0.682, respectively). (F) Kaplan-Meier survival curves comparing riskscore-high and riskscore-low groups in the GSE31210 validation cohort. AUC, area under the curve; CI, confidence interval; DEGGs, differentially expressed galactose metabolism-related genes; HR, hazard ratio; LUAD, lung adenocarcinoma; OS, overall survival; ROC, receiver operating characteristic.

sec.p: To assess the generalizability of the six-gene prognostic model, we performed external validation using the independent GSE31210 dataset (n=226). The model demonstrated predictive performance, with 1-, 3-, and 5-year AUC values for OS of 0.709, 0.691, and 0.682, respectively (Figure 4E). Kaplan-Meier analysis revealed significantly shorter OS in the high-risk group compared to the low-risk group (P<0.05), consistent with the findings in the TCGA cohort (Figure 4F).

sec.title: Risk score is associated with divergent immune infiltration patterns
sec.p: GSEA showed that immune-related pathways were significantly enriched in the low-risk group, including the regulation of natural killer (NK) cell-mediated immunity (NES =2.02, P=0.0002), immunoglobulin complex (NES =2.40, P<0.0001), immunoglobulin receptor binding (NES =2.36, P<0.0001), and immunoregulatory interactions between lymphoid and non-lymphoid cells (NES =1.43, P=0.0006) (Figure 5A-5D). Immune infiltration analysis revealed significant differences in 15 of 22 immune cell subsets between the two groups. Among these, 7 cell types (including M2 Macrophages, resting Mast cells, resting Dendritic cells, Tregs, activated NK cells, Monocytes, and memory B cells) displayed significant positive correlations with the risk scores. On the other hand, 8 cell types (plasma cells, M0 macrophages, CD8+ T cells, M1 macrophages, activated CD4+ memory T cells, Neutrophils, activated Mast cells, and resting NK cells) showed significant negative correlations with the risk scores (P<0.05) (Figure 5E). TIDE analysis indicated higher immune exclusion and poorer predicted immunotherapy response in the high-risk group (Figure 5F). Validation results from the GSE126044 dataset showed that the high-riskscore group exhibited a lower response to immunotherapy compared to the low-riskscore group (Figure 5G).

caption.p: Differences in immune infiltration between riskscore-high and riskscore-low patients. (A-D) The significantly enriched pathways in GSEA including the immunoregulatory interactions between lymphoid and non-lymphoid cells, immunoglobulin receptor binding, immunoglobulin complex, and regulation of NK cell-mediated immunity. (E) Tumor immune infiltration analysis of 22 immune cells. (F) TIDE analysis in riskscore-high LUAD patients compared to riskscore-low groups. (G) Validation of immunotherapy response based on high and low riskscores in the GSE126044 dataset. ns, not significant; *, P<0.05; **, P<0.01; ***, P<0.001; ****, P<0.0001. CAF, cancer-associated fibroblast; GSEA, gene set enrichment analysis; LUAD, lung adenocarcinoma; MDSC, myeloid-derived suppressor cell; NES, normalized enrichment score; NK, natural killer; TIDE, Tumor Immune Dysfunction and Exclusion.

sec.title: High expression of immune checkpoint genes in the high-risk group
sec.p: Differential expression analysis of 41 immune checkpoint genes demonstrated that BTLA, BTN2A1, BTN2A2, CD27, CD276, CD28, CD47, CD70, HLA-A, HLA-C, KIR2DL4, PVR, SIRPA, TDO2, TNFRSF18, TNFRSF9, TNFSF14, TNFSF15, TNFSF18, TNFSF4, and TNFSF9 were significantly positively correlated with risk scores, whereas BTNL9 showed a significant negative correlation (Figure 6A). Notably, HLA-A exhibited dual roles in our analyses: it was positively correlated with risk scores in the immune checkpoint gene set, consistent with its reported immunosuppressive function, but negatively correlated in the T-cell proliferation driver gene set, reflecting its role as a key antigen-presenting molecule. Analysis of 15 synthetic driver genes for T cell proliferation revealed that AHCY, BATF, CLIC1, DBI, GPN3, HLA-A, HOMER1, IL1RN, LIG3, MRPL18, MRPL51, NFYB, RAN, and ZNF830 were negatively correlated with risk scores, while GPD1 was positively correlated (Figure 6B). Furthermore, the expression levels of exhausted T cell markers were significantly elevated in the high-risk group compared to the low-risk group (Figure 6C). These results collectively suggest that patients in the high-risk group exhibit an impaired antitumor immune function.

sec.title: Elevated tumor stemness in the high-risk group
sec.p: The tumor stemness index was significantly higher in the high-risk group than in the low-risk group (Figure 6D). Additionally, stemness-related genes, including DNMT3B, EZH2, FOXA1, FOXP1, FOXP2, FOXP3, GLI2, HOXA10, HOXA11, HOXA3, HOXA7, HOXB3, HOXB5, HOXC10, HOXC6, HOXC8, HOXD10, HTR7, IRX4, MSX2, MYC, NFATC1, NOTCH2, NRF2, OLIG2, PAX9, PCNA, PITX2, PITX3, POU4F1, RB1, RUNX1, SIX2, SMAD2, SP1, STAT1, STAT3, VDR, WRN, and ZFPM2, were also expressed at higher levels in the riskscore-High group (Figure 6E). These stemness-related genes exhibited significantly higher expression in the riskscore-High group, particularly those involved in embryonic development, such as the HOX family genes, suggesting a more aggressive tumor phenotype in high-risk patients.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, we successfully identified six DEGs (GALT, GANC, B4GALT1, PGM1, PGM2, and GALM) and constructed a robust prognostic model for LUAD patients. Our model demonstrated excellent predictive performance for OS, with risk stratification revealing distinct immunological and stemness characteristics between high-risk and low-risk groups. This finding represents a significant advancement in understanding the interplay between galactose metabolism, tumor immunity, and clinical outcomes in LUAD.

The six-gene signature identified in our study provides novel insights into the regulatory mechanisms linking galactose metabolism to tumor immune microenvironment. Previous studies have primarily focused on galactose as a substrate for galactosylceramide synthesis, which regulates cell proliferation, angiogenesis, and apoptosis (23,24). However, the adverse clinical effects of galactose metabolism on the immune system remain poorly understood. Kelly’s seminal work in 1971 first proposed that galactose can inhibit the bactericidal activity of white blood cells, but the underlying mechanisms remained elusive (25).

Our findings significantly extend this knowledge by demonstrating that galactose metabolism-related genes are intricately involved in regulating immune cell infiltration and function. Specifically, low-risk patients exhibited significantly enriched pathways related to NK cell-mediated immunity, immunoglobulin complex formation, immunoglobulin receptor binding, and immunoregulatory interactions between lymphoid and non-lymphoid cells. This suggests that dysregulation of galactose metabolism may create an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, potentially through multiple mechanisms including altered glycosylation patterns and metabolic reprogramming of immune cells.

Among the six genes comprising our prognostic model, each demonstrates distinct functional roles in tumor biology and immune regulation. Recent studies have shown that GALT antibodies can enhance immune responses and promote anti-tumor immunity (26), suggesting its potential as an immunomodulatory target. B4GALT1 gene has been extensively studied in LUAD, where it regulates proliferation and invasion both in vitro and in vivo. Importantly, B4GALT1 has been shown to compromise CD8+ T cell anti-tumor functionality through direct mediation of N-linked glycosylation of PD-L1 proteins, thereby stabilizing PD-L1 and preventing its post-transcriptional degradation (27). This mechanism provides a direct link between galactose metabolism and immune checkpoint regulation. PGM1 and PGM2 phosphoglucomutase isoforms have been validated as prognostic markers in lung cancer and bladder cancer (28,29), highlighting their importance in cancer metabolism. Although GALM is has primarily been studied in glioma and clear cell renal cell carcinoma (30,31), our findings suggest its broader relevance for LUAD prognosis.

Notably, the regulatory effects of galactose metabolism on T cell proliferation-related genes and immune-related gene expression have not been previously reported, representing a significant novel finding of this study. Our work bridges the gap between cancer metabolism and tumor immunology, providing a comprehensive framework for understanding how metabolic reprogramming influences immune cell function in LUAD.

The tumor microenvironment exhibits upregulated Leloir pathway activity, which promotes the synthesis of immunosuppressive glycans such as sialylated Lewis X. These glycans engage Siglec receptors on immune cells to transduce inhibitory signals. Intriguingly, LacCer produced by β-1,4-GalT-V can paradoxically activate signaling pathways like NF-κB, leading to the recruitment of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and suppression of T-cell function, thereby favoring tumor progression. Systemically, circulating galactose reprograms hepatocyte metabolism by inactivating mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1), which induces the production of Insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 1 (IGFBP-1) to enhance CD8+ T cell function (32). The Leloir pathway serves as a central regulator of galactose metabolism, where key enzymes including GALE and UGDH maintain the UDP-galactose pool necessary for glycolipid and glycoprotein biosynthesis. This dual role—locally suppressing immunity in the tumor niche while systemically potentially enhancing T-cell activity—highlights the metabolic complexity of galactose handling in cancer immunity (33,34).

Galectin-1, highly expressed in aggressive cancer stem cells (CSCs) like glioma stem cells, promotes the Warburg effect via CA9 activation to support rapid proliferation and genomic integrity while modulating cell-cell interactions through its galactose recognition domain to maintain stem cell niche stability and drive tumor invasion (35). UDP-galactose serves as a critical substrate for protein glycosylation, with aberrant Leloir pathway enzyme expression (e.g., GALK1) acting as cancer biomarkers, while galactose metabolism influences NAD+/NADH ratios to indirectly regulate histone modifications and DNA methylation, sustaining pluripotency gene expression programs (36-38). Targeted inhibition of the Leloir pathway using galactose antimetabolites like UDP-4DFG, which blocks GALE and UGDH to disrupt galactose metabolic flux and glycan synthesis, effectively reverses CSCs stemness and reduces tumor cell viability, demonstrating the essential role of galactose metabolism in CSCs survival (39).

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, comprehensive bioinformatics analyses lacked in-depth functional validation, necessitating future experiments to elucidate molecular mechanisms of galactose metabolism-related genes in immune regulation and tumor stemness. Second, the predictive model showed moderate performance with AUC values of 0.719, 0.693, and 0.684 at 1-, 3-, and 5-year time points, respectively, declining over time and requiring optimization through larger samples and refined algorithms. Third, retrospective data may introduce selection/information bias, while LUAD subtype heterogeneity and varied treatment histories across datasets limit generalizability. Future validation in specific molecular subtypes and therapeutic contexts is essential to enhance clinical applicability.

Despite these limitations, our prognostic model based on galactose metabolism-related genes shows reliable predictive performance and is closely associated with immune infiltration, immune checkpoint expression, and tumor stemness. It may help identify LUAD patients who could benefit from immunotherapy and improve individualized risk stratification in clinical practice.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Our prognostic model, based on six galactose metabolism-related genes, demonstrates that patients in the riskscore-Low LUAD exhibit a more favorable prognosis, characterized by a higher diversity of tumor-infiltrating immune cells and a more active anti-tumor immune response. These findings provide valuable insights for the personalized immunotherapy of LUAD patients, as the model can potentially guide clinical decisions and provide effective monitoring for personalized treatment.
